literal:
The Historical Setting Before the Flood

Genesis 6 presents the historical circumstances leading to the great Deluge. The chapter opens with the mysterious account of the "sons of God" taking wives from among the "daughters of men," resulting in the birth of the Nephilim or giants. This passage has occasioned much debate among the Fathers and theologians.

The "Sons of God" Controversy

Two principal interpretations have been advanced by Catholic tradition:

The Sethite Interpretation: St. Augustine, in his City of God (Book XV, chapters 22-23), argues that the "sons of God" were the righteous descendants of Seth, while the "daughters of men" were women from the corrupt lineage of Cain. Augustine writes that "by these two names (sons of God and daughters of men) the two cities are sufficiently distinguished. For though the former were by nature children of men, they had come into possession of another name by grace." This interpretation was also held by Julius Africanus, Theodoret of Cyrus, and Cyril of Alexandria, and it became the dominant view through the medieval period.

Theodoret of Cyrus explains: "His intention was to annihilate Cain's line, but since the tribe of the virtuous had intermarried with Cain's line, it was also involved in the punishment. Wanting to make a beginning of a new way of life, he preserved Noah and his sons along with their wives, for Noah was good and righteous."

The Angelic Interpretation: Some earlier Fathers, following Jewish tradition found in texts like 1 Enoch, held that the "sons of God" referred to angelic beings who transgressed their proper boundaries. While this view has ancient attestation, Augustine's Sethite interpretation prevailed in later Catholic tradition.

The Corruption of Humanity

Verses 5-7 describe God's grief over human wickedness: "And God seeing that the wickedness of men was great on the earth, and that all the thought of their heart was bent upon evil at all times, it repented him that he had made man on the earth. And being touched inwardly with sorrow of heart, He said: I will destroy man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth." The Hebrew text emphasizes the totality of human corruption—not merely external acts, but the very imagination and intent of the heart was continually evil.

Noah Finds Grace

In stark contrast stands Noah: "But Noah found grace before the Lord" (v. 8). The text describes him as "a just man and perfect in his generations" who "walked with God" (v. 9). Pseudo-Basil of Caesarea notes that "Noah spent a hundred years working on the ark and the people would not turn away from their sins. Even when he came to seven days and he tried once more to warn them... they did not do so at all."

The Ark's Specifications

God commands Noah to build the ark with precise dimensions: 300 cubits in length, 50 cubits in breadth, and 30 cubits in height (approximately 450 x 75 x 45 feet). The ark was to have three stories, a door in its side, and an opening for light near the top, finished "a cubit above." It was to be made of "gopher wood" (likely cypress) and pitched within and without. St. Jerome clarifies verse 3: "So human life is not reduced to 120 years, as many erroneously presumed, but 120 years was given for repentance to that generation."
allegorical:
The Ark as Type of the Church

From the earliest centuries, the Church Fathers recognized Noah's ark as a profound type of the Church of Christ. This typology has explicit Scriptural warrant in 1 Peter 3:20-21, where the Apostle writes that in the ark "a few, that is, eight souls, were saved by water. Whereunto baptism being of the like form, now saveth you also."

Patristic Testimony

St. Cyprian of Carthage (d. 258) established the classic formulation: "He can no longer have God for his Father who has not the Church for his mother. If any one could escape who was outside the Ark of Noah, then he also may escape who shall be outside of the Church." He further writes: "The one ark of Noah was a type of the one Church. If, then, in that baptism of the world thus expiated and purified, he who was not in the ark of Noah could be saved by water, he who is not in the Church to which alone baptism is granted, can also now be quickened by baptism."

St. Jerome declares: "This is the ark of Noah, and he who is not found in it shall perish when the flood prevails."

St. John Chrysostom summarizes the typology: "The ark is the Church, Noah is Christ, the dove is the Holy Spirit, the olive branch is the divine charity. Thus as the ark in the midst of the sea protected those who found shelter inside it, so the Church saves all those who had gone astray. However, the ark only protected; the Church does more."

The Dimensions and the Body of Christ

St. Augustine, in City of God (Book XV, chapter 26), titled "That the Ark Which Noah Was Ordered to Make Figures In Every Respect Christ and the Church," writes that the ark "is certainly a figure of the city of God sojourning in this world; that is to say, of the church, which is rescued by the wood on which hung the Mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus."

Augustine finds profound significance in the ark's proportions: "Even its very dimensions, in length, breadth, and height, represent the human body in which He came... the length of the human body, from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot, is six times its breadth from side to side, and ten times its depth or thickness, measuring from back to front... if you measure a man as he lies on his back or on his face, he is six times as long from head to foot as he is broad from side to side, and ten times as long as he is high from the ground. And therefore the ark was made 300 cubits in length, 50 in breadth, and 30 in height." The ark thus prefigures the Body of Christ—both His physical body and His Mystical Body, the Church.

The Wood and the Cross

St. Ambrose, in his work On the Mysteries, connects the wood of the ark with the wood of the Cross: "You see the water, you see the wood [of the ark], you see the dove, and do you hesitate as to the mystery?" He continues: "The water, then, is that in which the flesh is dipped, that all carnal sin may be washed away. All wickedness is there buried. The wood is that on which the Lord Jesus was fastened when He suffered for us."

Augustine similarly teaches that the ark "represents the primary means of salvation in the New Testament—the wood of the cross and the waters of baptism by which original sin is washed away."

The Door in the Side

Augustine sees in the door on the ark's side a figure of Christ's wounded side on the Cross: "Its having a door made in the side of it certainly signified the wound which was made when the side of the Crucified was pierced with the spear; for by this those who come to Him enter; for thence flowed the sacraments by which those who believe are initiated." From Christ's side flowed blood and water—the Eucharist and Baptism—by which we enter the Church.

The Structure of the Ark

The three stories of the ark have been variously interpreted. Augustine suggests they may represent "the two kinds of men—the circumcision, to wit, and the uncircumcision, or, as the apostle otherwise calls them, Jews and Gentiles," or alternatively "the three graces commended by the apostle—faith, hope, and charity." The squared timbers from which it was built "signify the immoveable steadiness of the life of the saints; for however you turn a cube, it still stands."

Augustine also notes that the ark was "finished in a cubit above," which he interprets as signifying how "the Church, the body of Christ gathered into unity, is raised to perfection."

Noah as Type of Christ

Noah himself prefigures Christ. As the Catholic Encyclopedia states: "In the Fathers and tradition he is considered as the type and figure of the Saviour, because through him the human race was saved from destruction and reconciled with God." As Noah built the ark, the only means of salvation from the Deluge, so Christ established the Church, the only means of salvation in the spiritual order.
moral:
Noah's Righteousness Amid Corruption

The tropological or moral sense of Genesis 6 concerns the virtues by which Noah found favor with God and the lessons his example offers for the Christian life.

The Character of Noah

Scripture describes Noah with three distinct praises: he was "a just man," he was "perfect in his generations," and he "walked with God" (v. 9). These indicate, respectively, his righteousness in dealings with others, his integrity of life, and his intimate communion with the Lord. As St. Peter later attests, Noah was "a herald of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5).

The phrase "perfect in his generations" does not indicate sinlessness but rather wholeness and integrity. As one commentator notes, the word "blameless" in Hebrew "denotes an animal that is acceptable for a sacrifice." Noah was wholly devoted to God in an age when such devotion was rare. He had "a heart to seek God and he lived his life in accordance with God's standards of morality."

Righteousness in a Corrupt Generation

Noah's righteousness is remarkable precisely because of the context in which he lived. When "all the thought of their heart was bent upon evil at all times" and "the earth was corrupted before God, and was filled with iniquity" (v. 5, 11), Noah stood apart. He demonstrates that faithfulness to God is possible even when surrounded by wickedness.

Athanasius presents the tragedy of the sons of Seth as "a moral lesson about compromise: godly men intermarrying with a wicked generation, leading to spiritual downfall." The moral teaching is clear: the righteous must guard against the corrupting influence of the world. As St. Paul would later warn: "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners" (1 Corinthians 15:33).

Obedience to God's Unusual Commands

God commanded Noah to undertake an extraordinary task—to build a massive vessel on dry land in preparation for an unprecedented flood. St. John Chrysostom, in his homilies on Genesis, urges us not to "question the actions of God with human reason." Noah's faith enabled him to obey a command that must have seemed incomprehensible to his contemporaries, and which likely occasioned their mockery.

The Epistle to the Hebrews commends this faith: "By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house; by the which he condemned the world, and became heir of the righteousness which is by faith" (Hebrews 11:7). Noah believed God's warning about "things not seen as yet" and acted accordingly. His obedience thus became itself a testimony against an unbelieving world.

Patience and Perseverance

Pseudo-Basil of Caesarea notes that "Noah spent a hundred years working on the ark and the people would not turn away from their sins." Throughout this extended period of labor, Noah persevered in his task without wavering. He models the virtue of patient endurance in well-doing, trusting that God's promised salvation would come in its appointed time.

Preparation for Judgment

Noah's example teaches the necessity of preparation. God gave warning of coming judgment, and Noah responded by making ready. For the Christian, this means living in a state of readiness for death and judgment, cultivating virtue, avoiding sin, and remaining in a state of grace. As Christ Himself would later warn: "As in the days of Noah, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be" (Matthew 24:37). Those who dismissed Noah's warnings perished; those who heeded them were saved.

God's Tender Care for the Righteous

When Noah and his family entered the ark, "the Lord shut him in" (Genesis 7:16). St. John Chrysostom sees in this detail an example of God's tender care: "Notice in this place too the considerateness in the expression... to teach us that he had ensured the good man's complete safety." God does not merely command obedience; He also provides protection and care for those who obey.
anagogical:
The Flood as Type of Final Judgment

The anagogical sense of Scripture points to the ultimate realities—the Last Things, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the final consummation of all things. Genesis 6 and the flood narrative richly anticipate the eschatological judgment that awaits the world.

Christ's Own Testimony

Our Lord Himself established the typological connection between the flood and His Second Coming: "And as in the days of Noah, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be. For as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noah entered into the ark, and knew not until the flood came, and took them all away; so shall also the coming of the Son of man be" (Matthew 24:37-39; cf. Luke 17:26-27).

This dominical teaching established for the Church that "the flood narrative, inspired by God, prophetically prepares us for the future and turns our gaze not to past history but to the future eschaton." The first universal judgment by water prefigures the last universal judgment by fire.

The Pattern of Judgment and Salvation

The theology of the universal Flood reveals a pattern that will be repeated at the end: "world-wide creation revealing the character of the Creator; humankind's turning from the Creator and the universal spread of sin ending in the universal 'uncreation' through eschatological judgment; and re-creation, in the eschatological salvation of the faithful covenant remnant and the universal renewal of the earth."

St. Peter explicitly draws this parallel: "For this they willingly are ignorant of, that by the word of God the heavens were of old, and the earth standing out of the water and in the water: whereby the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished: but the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men" (2 Peter 3:5-7).

The Saved Remnant

In the flood, only eight souls were saved—Noah, his wife, his three sons, and their wives. This small remnant preserved through judgment prefigures the elect who will be saved through the final tribulation. As Christ warned: "Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it" (Matthew 7:13-14).

The ark itself, as St. Thomas Aquinas teaches, signifies that "there is no entering into salvation outside the Church, just as in the time of the deluge there was none outside the Ark." Christ becomes "an ark of refuge and safety to His people through the fiery judgment to come. He is the temple of God, the place of God's presence, the sanctuary of His people and their new 'eschatological-ark.'"

The New Creation

After the flood, creation emerged renewed. St. John Chrysostom writes that creation's "countenance was made resplendent" following the cleansing of the flood. The new world after the Deluge, with Noah's family as the new humanity and the rainbow covenant as sign of God's faithfulness, prefigures the new heavens and new earth promised in Revelation: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away" (Revelation 21:1).

The flood narrative "ends in new creation" and contains "creation numerology, most significantly the presence of the number seven"—the number of completion and rest. As the ark rested on the mountains of Ararat and Noah emerged into a purified world, so the elect will enter into the eternal rest of the new creation after the final judgment.

The Certainty of Judgment

The antediluvian generation was given warning through Noah's preaching and the visible sign of the ark being built, yet they "knew not until the flood came." Their willful ignorance did not exempt them from judgment. So too, at the end, "the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, to execute judgment upon all" (Jude 14-15).

Gregory of Nazianzus described Noah as one "entrusted with the saving of the whole world from the waters." In the anagogical sense, Christ is the true Noah, who saves His Church through the waters of baptism now and will bring her safely through the final judgment to the eternal kingdom prepared from the foundation of the world.
